flashcards.q: What are the three mandatory follow-ups asked after EVERY story in this round, regardless of how good it sounds?
flashcards.a: 1) 'Give me the number, and how you measured it.' 2) 'What did you consider and not do, and what did that alternative cost you?' 3) 'What would you do differently if you did it again tomorrow?'

flashcards.q: What's the asymmetric time shape of a single STAR answer?
flashcards.a: Situation 10% (~15s), Task 10% (~15s), Action 50% (~90s), Result 15% (~25s), rejected alternative 10% (~20s), redo/retrospective 5% (~10s). Action is where the score lives.

flashcards.q: Why is a story with no number scored at the bottom of the rubric regardless of how well it's told?
flashcards.a: Because the Result section requires a number with a stated measurement method to be verifiable evidence rather than a claim -- a well-told story with no number is indistinguishable from a well-told fabrication.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between 'claimed' and 'assigned' work, and why does it matter for level calibration?
flashcards.a: Assigned: 'my manager asked me to migrate the batch job' (senior work). Claimed: 'I noticed X was costing us Y and proposed and ran the fix' (staff work) -- same project, different level. Mark your own stories A/C and lead with the C ones at staff+.

flashcards.q: What number in this student's own story bank is explicitly flagged as the most attackable claim, and why?
flashcards.a: The ~25% engagement uplift figure -- a Bar Raiser is trained to find exactly this kind of bare percentage with no stated denominator, baseline, comparison design (holdout vs pre/post), or confounders named.

flashcards.q: What's the honest answer if a metric was measured via pre/post comparison with no holdout, and why does admitting it score higher than inventing rigor?
flashcards.a: Say so plainly and name why a holdout wasn't available (tenant contracts, rollout mechanics, no experimentation platform). Fabricated specificity about methodology collapses under one more question; honest limitation does not.

flashcards.q: What's a 'disguised praise' retrospective, and why does it fail the 'what would you do differently' question?
flashcards.a: A restatement of what already went well dressed up as humility ('I'd probably do the exact same thing, it worked out great'). It fails because a real retrospective must cost something to admit -- a specific, non-trivial revision, not affirmation of the original decision.

flashcards.q: Why does inflating a single-team story to cross-team/org-wide scope collapse quickly, and what's the safer move?
flashcards.a: It collapses on 'which teams, and what did they want?' -- an unanswerable follow-up if the scope was invented. Safer: state scope honestly, including admitting a story is single-team, since honest scope survives scrutiny and inflated scope does not.

flashcards.q: How does the interviewer's drilling style change by default company lens (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Netflix)?
flashcards.a: Amazon: Bar Raiser drills for depth until something breaks. Google: demands quotable, transcribable sentences (a committee reads written notes, never met you). Meta: demands compression + multi-team scope + ends on self-critique. Microsoft: tracks your weakest answer for a second pass (AA round). Netflix: expects peer-level candor with no scaffolding.

flashcards.q: Why is 'we decided to self-host and it worked well' scored lower than 'I benchmarked three instance families against the real request distribution'?
flashcards.a: The first is first-person-plural with no isolable personal contribution ('team narration'); the second is first-person-singular with a specific, verifiable mechanism. Personal ownership vs. team narration is the single most common reason a strong-sounding story scores low.

flashcards.q: What's the required, prepared 2026 answer this round tests, and what does a weak version of it look like?
flashcards.a: How you work with AI coding tools, with a category rule (accept lightly reviewed vs. verify-deeply) and one concrete override instance. Weak: 'I always review AI-generated code carefully' with no category rule and no real instance.

flashcards.q: Why should you never criticize a current or former employer, even when a criticism is factually justified?
flashcards.a: It reads as a risk signal regardless of justification, and it devalues every other story told in the same round that was built on that employer's platform -- criticizing the employer criticizes the evidence base of the whole round.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between the LEAN HIRE band (9-12/20) and the HIRE band (13-16/20) in this round?
flashcards.a: LEAN HIRE: stories are real and personally owned but numbers are frequently bare (no denominator/baseline) and the rejected-alternative/retrospective are thin even after being asked directly. HIRE: STAR shape solid, mandatory follow-ups produce real answers, but 1-2 need the follow-up prompt to surface rather than being volunteered.

flashcards.q: Why is repeating the same headline story unchanged across multiple competency questions a time-management failure?
flashcards.a: It reads as a thin story bank even when the underlying story is strong. Fix: explicit reframing ('I mentioned the platform earlier for ownership; let me take the security angle this time').

flashcards.q: What single red flag is worse than a low score on any individual story?
flashcards.a: Naming a Leadership Principle or competency explicitly while telling the story ('this really shows my ownership') instead of simply exhibiting the behavior -- narrating the rubric instead of meeting it.
